[?] By the same author: A discourse of exhortation to Stagirius, an ascetic possessed by a demon. Book One.

1. I ought, Stagirius, dearest of all to me, to be with you now and share your distress, and to [?] [?] consolatory discourse 1. In Morel: By the same, a discourse [?] to Stagirius, an ascetic possessed by a demon, book [?]

lighten it as far as I could. But my bodily weakness, and the illness that has struck my head and forced me to stay at home, have deprived me of a service that would bring so much gain. So what is left to me, both for your consolation and for my own benefit, I will not hesitate to offer as well as I can. Perhaps it will help you a little to bear your present troubles nobly. And if I achieve nothing of the kind, at least the knowledge that I left undone nothing in my power will make me easier in mind from now on. For whoever has done everything he thinks may help release a friend from the miseries that hold him is at least freed from his own conscience's reproach, even if he accomplishes nothing. He has put down the burden of blame and has only the burden of sorrow left to bear. If I were one of those who are pleasing to God and have great power with him, I would not stop begging and imploring him on behalf of the person so precious to me. But my many sins have stripped me of that boldness and that strength, so I will try to offer you the comfort of words instead. With people who are sick in body, it is the physicians' work to take away the pain and end the disease. But even the servants who look after the sick are not barred from comforting them. In fact they are the ones who spend the most words on this, when they are loyal to their masters. If I say something that can quench this boundless pain, what I pray for has happened. If I find nothing of the kind to say, he will surely accept my good will at least, the one who commanded through blessed Paul that we weep with those who weep and associate with the lowly. Now it seems to you that the one cause of your sorrow is the frenzy of this wicked demon. But one could find many griefs, one after another, springing from this root. I am not saying this on my own account. It comes from what I often heard you lament to me when you were with me. First, while you were living a more worldly life in earlier days you suffered nothing like this, but once you had crucified yourself to the world, then you began to feel the disease. That alone is enough to disturb a man and throw him into perplexity. Second, many who suffered the same affliction as you, even people who lived in luxury, held out for a short time and were freed from this illness. They returned to such complete health that they married, became fathers of many children, enjoyed the pleasures of this present life, and never suffered anything like it again. You, on the other hand, have spent so long in fasting, all-night vigils and every other austerity, and have found no release from the terrible things that grip you. Third, that holy man, who had shown such power in the case of other men, could do nothing of the sort for you, my dear friend, and neither could those with him, though they were more powerful than he. All alike went away blushing. Besides these, you said that something else pained you terribly: that your soul's [?] [?]. εὖνοι ("well-disposed"): Savile; εὔνοοι, [?] Colbert codex. δύναμις ("power"): Savile in the text [?]. τυραννίς ("tyranny"). Next, Morel: "often to come to the noose." [?] we follow.

terrible, and nothing pleasant was pleasant to me. I had long since condemned the great vanity of the things of this life, but I felt it far more then, and a greater longing for your devout company came over me. Such is the nature of misfortune: it always strengthens friendships. This is clear from the fact that it can easily dissolve even enmities. No one is so wretched or so stupid that he can keep up his hostility toward an enemy when he sees him suffering. If we pity our enemies and make friends of them when we see that they have suffered something unwished for, think what I was likely to feel when I saw the dearest of all to me, whom I value as much as my own life, in incurable straits so far as his sorrow is concerned. Do not think that I stand outside your affliction, and do not distrust my words of comfort on that account. By God's grace I am spared being convulsed and thrown down by the wicked demon, but I bear an equal share with you of the sorrow and pain it brings. No one who knows how to love as one ought to love would disbelieve me. Come then, let us shake off the dust. That way the nature of this sorrow will become bearable and light, provided we do not simply hand ourselves over to the passion and let ourselves be dragged over the cliffs, but make an effort to come to our senses and work out something of what is needed. Many things that seem terrible look great and unbearable before they are properly examined. But if someone looks at them closely with his reason, he will find them much smaller than he supposed. I hope that will happen now too. So rouse yourself. Do not follow the empty and irrational opinion of the crowd and so make the enemy fiercer against us. If I were speaking to an unbeliever, or to one of those who think everything happens by chance, or to those who attribute the government of the world to evil demons, I would need a great deal of work. I would first have to drive out the mistaken opinion and persuade him to recognize the true providence over all things, and only then turn my discourse to consolation. But by God's grace you have known the sacred writings from infancy. You received the true and saving doctrines from your forefathers, and you believe firmly that God cares for all things, and especially for those who believe in him. So let us leave that part aside and begin from another point. When God made the angels... or rather, let us take the argument further back. Before the angels came into being, and the other powers in the heavens, God existed, and his existence never had a beginning. He has always been without need, for such is the Divine, and yet he made angels, archangels and the other incorporeal beings. He made them for no other reason than his goodness alone. He did not need their service, and he would not have become their creator unless he were exceedingly good. After creating them, he made man too, again for this same reason, and this whole world. He filled the world with countless good things and set that small and paltry creature over works so great, appointing him to be on earth what he himself is in the heavens. [?] For [?] [?] Morel: μεῖζόν με πάθος ("a greater passion [came over] me"), less correctly. [?] Savile in the margin: μὴ συγχωρήσωμεν ("let us not allow"), and next τῷ πάθει φέρεσθαι ("to be carried along by the passion").

[?] I would say nothing, since it is plain to everyone. But I must give an account of what came afterward.

3. How then shall we know that the later events were also for his good? We shall know it if we consider what he would have suffered had they not happened. What then would he have suffered? After the transgression, when the devil had promised to make them equal to God, suppose Adam had kept the same honor. He would have fallen into three of the worst evils. First, he would have thought God envious, a deceiver and a liar. Second, he would have thought the one who really is a deceiver, the father of lies and of envy, to be his benefactor and friend. Third, he would have gone on sinning forever after, never dying. God freed him from all of these by driving him out of paradise at that time. In the same way a physician who leaves a sore alone makes the rot worse, but by cutting it out he stops the infection of the wound from spreading further. "What then?" someone says. "God did not stop there. He added sweat and toil as well." He did so because nothing is so badly suited to ease as human nature. Even with these burdens laid on us we do not stop sinning. What would we not have dared if God had let us loose to luxury and idleness? "Idleness," Scripture says, "has taught every evil." What happens every day bears out the saying, and so does what befell our forefathers. "The people sat down to eat and drink," it says, "and rose up to play." And again: "He grew fat, he grew thick, he grew sleek, and the beloved kicked." Blessed David says the same: "When he slew them, then they sought him, and turned and came early to God." And to Jerusalem God says through Jeremiah: "Be disciplined at all times, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you." Being humbled and bent is good for salvation, and not only for the wicked but also for the good. Again the prophet says so: "It is good for me, Lord, that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes." After him Jeremiah cries out the same thing, though not in the same words: "It is good for a man to bear a heavy yoke from his youth. He will sit alone and keep silent." And for himself he begs God: "Do not spare me, to my estrangement, in an evil day." Blessed Paul shone so brightly in grace that he rose above human nature, yet he too needed the benefit of this good. That is why he said: "A thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet me, so that I might not be too elated. Three times I begged the Lord about this, and he said to me: My grace is enough for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Indeed, the preaching could have succeeded without persecutions, afflictions, toil and sweat. Yet Christ chose not to spare his preachers. That is why he tells them: "In the world you will have affliction." And he commands those who wish to walk into the kingdom to go by the narrow road, since there is no other way to get there. So afflictions, trials and the griefs that come upon us show God's care for us no less than good things do. And why do I speak of afflictions? [?] Savile: οὐδ' ἂν εἴποιμι ("nor would I say"). So Morel. [?] besides these, and leading to repentance, of which [?]

and an unrepentant heart, has stored up wrath for himself, then God proceeds against him. If Cain had remained unpunished even after the murder, he would have gone on to some other, greater evil. Nor can anyone say that he sinned out of ignorance. What his younger brother understood, how could he not have known? But if you like, let us grant that the first offense came from ignorance. After he heard "Be still," after he had received pardon, what ignorance led him on to murder, to defile the earth and overturn the laws of nature? Do you see that even the earlier offense did not come from ignorance, but from vice, malice and the worst depravity? What then was his punishment for all this? "You shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth." The punishment seems harsh. But it is not, if we weigh the sin and examine the punishment itself carefully. When he made his offering badly, he resented that God, whom he had insulted, did not honor him. He spurned God when God admonished him. He was the first to dare murder, or rather a pollution far more accursed than murder. He grieved his parents. He lied to God: "Am I my brother's keeper?" he says. And in return for all this he is punished only with fear and trembling. Still, I would say that God's kindness shows itself not only in the punishment being milder than the sin, but also in its bringing no ordinary gain. The gain was that everyone who came after was chastened and became better through the rebuke given to him. That is why God did not kill him. It was not the same thing to hear that a certain Cain killed his brother and died as to see the killer paying the penalty. In the first case the story might have been disbelieved because the abomination was so extreme. As it was, he was visible and present, and over a long time he made many people witnesses of his punishment, and so he made the deed plain and credible both to the people of that time and to those who came after. "What has this to do with Cain himself?" someone says. A great deal. First, God provided for his salvation too, when he tried beforehand to check his madness, as far as it lay with God, by admonishing him in words. And if one examines the punishment itself, one will see that it too brought much benefit. If God had killed him at once, he would have given him no time for repentance and amendment. As it was, he lived with trembling and fear, and unless he was utterly insensible, more beast than man, he could have gained much from that life. Besides this, through this punishment God made his future punishment lighter. The griefs and chastisements God brings on us in the present life cut off no small part of the torments there. One can bring evidence of this from the divine Scriptures. Christ, speaking with his disciples and telling the story of Lazarus, says that when the rich man begged Abraham for a little drop from the tip of a finger on his burning tongue, Abraham said to him: "Child, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus his bad things. Now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish." And Paul (when I say Paul, I am again speaking of Christ's commands, for Christ moved that blessed soul), writing once to the Corinthians about the [?] Savile: ἐφ' ἕτερον μεῖζον ἂν προῆλθε δεινόν ("would have gone on to another, greater terrible thing"). Savile: ὅτε γὰρ προσήνεγκε ("for when he offered"). Colbert: ὅρα γὰρ προσενέγκαι ("for see, to offer").

For in this way the good man was harmed because of the wicked one, but the wicked one is wicked not because of the noble one but because of his own wickedness. For now these people seem to be raising a question about the devil. But if their argument is followed through, it will accuse and find fault with God's providence in many things, and slander the whole of God's creation. It will find fault with the way the mouth and the eyes were formed. Through the eyes many people desire what they should not and fall into adultery. Through the mouth others blaspheme and put forward ruinous doctrines. Should human beings then have been made without tongues and eyes for this reason? Then let us cut off our feet too and chop off our hands, since the hands are full of blood and the feet run to evil. Nor will the ears escape the harshness of this argument, since they take in idle talk and pass corrupt doctrines on to the soul. So we will remove them as well. And if that is so, we must also do away with food and drink, heaven and earth, sea and sun, light and moon, the chorus of the stars, and every kind of animal. What use will these things be once the one for whose sake all things were made has been so pitifully mutilated? Do you see the absurdity and nonsense this argument is forced to end in? The devil is evil to himself, not to us. If we choose, we will reap many good things through him, though against his will and wishes. And in this the wonder is even greater, and so is the overflowing love of God for mankind. That people become better bites and grieves the devil in itself. But when this is brought about for us through him, he cannot bear the insult. How then is it brought about through him? We fear his cruelty, his constant plots and his endless schemes, so we shake off heavy sleep, we stay sober, and we remember the Lord at all times. And to show that this is not my own idea but blessed Paul's, listen to how he rouses the sleepers among the faithful in almost the same words. Writing to the Ephesians, he says something like this: "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places." He said this not to cast them down but to rouse them. And Peter says: "Be sober, be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, looking for someone to devour. Resist him, firm in the faith." He said this because he wanted to make them more vigorous and to persuade them to draw closer to God. For whoever sees the enemy standing over him runs all the more to the one who can help him and clings to him. Little children do the same. When they see something frightening, they run to their mother's bosom and hang on her clothes, holding on tightly. Even when many people pull at them, they often do not let go. But when there is nothing to frighten them, they will not put up with her calling and drawing them to her. They even scorn her when she calls, and turn away when she tries every means to draw them to her, and when the table is set [?] [?] Savile in the text ἐπηρεάσθη ("was harmed"), in the margin ἐπηρεάζεσθαι ("to be harmed").

Is this then all we can say about the flood, and shall we find no gain that came from it? On the contrary, one could not say how much it brought, both to those who died in it and to those born after them. The first were prevented from going further in wickedness. Those who came after them gained even more, because the leaven, so to speak, and the source of the evils had been removed from among them along with the very men who had committed them. If people can easily find out evils even without an example, what would they not have done with many others urging them on to wicked deeds? To keep this from happening, and so that later generations would not have so many teachers of vice, God destroyed them all utterly.

5. But what is the clever argument (or rather the foolish one) of those who want to do nothing good, but look for anything to say that will shift the blame for their own sins onto God? "If God had not permitted it," they say, "the devil would not have approached, nor would he have deceived anyone in the beginning." But then neither would Adam have learned how great a good he possessed, nor would he ever have come down from that madness of his. A man who thought himself worthy of so much that he expected to become a god, what would he not have dared if he had not been brought to his senses? But let us suppose that the devil had given no advice at all and had never spoken with Eve about the tree. If that had not happened, would they have gone on without falling? One cannot say so. A man so easily persuaded by his wife would soon have fallen into sin on his own, even if there had been no devil, and that would have made his punishment greater. Besides, even as things are, the devil's deceit is not the whole story. The woman fell because she was also caught by her own desire. Scripture indicated this when it said: "And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and pleasing to the eyes to look at, and lovely to contemplate; and she took of its fruit and ate." I am not saying this now to clear the devil of the charge of plotting against them. I want to show that if they had not fallen willingly, no one could have thrown them down. Anyone who accepts deception from another so easily was already careless and slack before he was deceived. The devil would not have had such power if he had been talking to a sober and wakeful soul. But there are some who, once refuted on this point, leave the devil aside and move on to the commandment. They leave the sinner alone and accuse God, saying: "Why did he give a command when he knew they would sin?" These too are the devil's words, the inventions of an impious mind. That giving the commandment showed greater care than not giving it is clear from the following. Suppose Adam had a will as careless as the outcome showed, but received no commandment and stayed in his life of luxury. Would that ease have made his weakness and carelessness worse or better? Clearly anyone can see that, with nothing to worry about, he would have fallen into the depths of wickedness. He did not yet have any confidence about immortality and knew that this hope was still uncertain. Yet he was lifted up to such arrogance and folly that he hoped to become a god, though he could see nothing to show that the one who promised this could be trusted. If he had possessed a secure immortality, where would he not have [?] Morel: ἀσεβοῦς ἐννοίας ("of an impious mind"). Savile: ἀσεβοῦς διανοίας ("of an impious understanding").

…we know of no other example of extreme tender love greater than this. But Isaiah taught something even greater. He took as his illustration the mother, who is far more compassionate toward her children than the father, and says: “Will a woman forget her child, or fail to have pity on the offspring of her womb? But even if a woman should forget these, I will not forget you, says the Lord.” He shows that God’s mercy is higher even than natural affection. So much for the prophets. Christ himself, speaking to the Jews, said: “If you, then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” By these words he shows nothing other than this: the difference between God’s care and a father’s care is as great as the distance between the good and the wicked. And do not stop even there, but go still further in your thinking, for this too has been said only so far as you are able to hear it. His understanding is infinite, and so is his goodness, and clearly so is his love for humankind. If we do not perceive it in each thing that happens, this too is a sign of its infinity. Every day many great things are arranged for our salvation that are evident to him alone. He benefits our race out of goodness, needing no glory from us and requiring no other return, and so he lets most of these things escape our notice. If he ever does reveal them, he does this too for our sake, so that we may become grateful and draw down still more of his help. Let us therefore thank him not only for the things we know, but also for those we do not know, for he knows how to do us good not only when we are willing, but also when we are unwilling. Paul knew this, and so he urged us to give thanks always and in all things. That God cares not only for all in common but also for each person individually, we can again hear from Christ himself, who says: “It is not the will of my Father in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” He is speaking of those who believe in him. For he wishes even those who do not believe in him to be saved, all of them, by changing and coming to faith, as Paul too says: “Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” And he himself said to the Jews: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance”; and again through the prophet: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” But even when, after enjoying such great care, they refuse to become better and acknowledge the truth, he does not abandon them even then. Since they have willingly deprived themselves of the heavenly life, he at least supplies them with everything for the present life: he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, sends rain on the just and the unjust, and provides everything else that sustains the present life. If he takes such forethought for his enemies, how could he ever overlook those who believe in him and serve him as far as they are able? It is not so, it is not so! Rather, he holds them in greater concern than all others. “For even the hairs of your head,” he says, “are all numbered.” [?] … “That one is coming [?]. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits, and we will say that an evil beast has devoured him; and

we shall see what will become of his dreams.” After this, those who had bought him sold him again, and not to a free man either, but to a royal slave. Nor did his troubles stop there. He fell victim to the false accusation of his mistress, was condemned, and lived in prison for many years; and when others got out, he stayed there longer still. Yet although so many things could have troubled his soul, he remained unshaken by them all. Our situation is like this, or rather far more perplexing. What God promised is the kingdom of heaven, eternal life, incorruption, and countless good things. But what happens to us in the meantime is far removed from these: death and decay, punishment and chastisement, and afflictions of every kind that never stop. Why then does God do this, and allow the opposite of his promises to come about? He accomplishes two very great things. First, he gives us indisputable proof of his power: even out of hopeless situations he can bring his promises to fulfillment. Second, he trains our soul to trust him in everything, even when what happens seems contrary to what was promised. Such is the strength of hope: it does not put to shame the one who holds to it sincerely. If those who received their promises here in this life were so disposed, how much more ought we to be, who await the fulfillment of the good things not in the present life but in other ages? For what he foretold for this life is affliction and distress. What is it, then, that troubles you? Why do you suspect God’s promise? To despise the whole world for his sake and then say that he has neglected you is nothing other than the mark of one who disbelieves, suspects, and thinks that promise a deception. That is truly to be possessed by a demon and to invite the fire of Gehenna. “But there are some who are wrapped up in worldly affairs and live in ease.” Christ foretold this too: “Truly, truly, I say to you,” he says, “you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.” In earlier generations, too, the Babylonians, who did not even know God, lived in wealth, power, and honor, while the Jews lived in captivity, slavery, and the worst of evils. And Lazarus, who was worthy of heaven and of the kingdom there, lay covered with sores, exposed to the tongues of dogs, battling constant hunger, while the rich man lived in honor, surrounded by attendants, in ease and luxury. Yet the rich man gained nothing [?] from these things in Gehenna, and Lazarus was not harmed by his hunger and his wounds with respect to the [?] of the present life. Like a noble athlete wrestling in drought and stifling heat, he both conquered and was crowned. For this reason a wise man says: “My son, if you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for testing. Set your heart right and endure, and do not be hasty in the time of calamity.” A little later he says: “Gold is tested in fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.” And again elsewhere he says: “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, and do not lose heart when he rebukes you.” For the one who throws gold into the furnace knows how long it must be heated and when it should be drawn out [?] … [?] such people. Below, in the same [manuscript] alone, “me” is read after “raised up.” Morel: “in poverty; and the other, by being forced and being disposed [?].”

…makes them more steadfast [?] and more devout. In short, anyone who wished to count them all would find that trials bring many gains. No one whom God holds in high regard is free from affliction, even if it does not seem so to us. 7. If blessed Paul endured this in full measure, and no one is greater than he, or even his equal, how could others not need this help? And if some were not brought to their senses even by these afflictions, the fault no longer lies with the one who applied the discipline, but with their own negligence. If the remedy had not been applied, they might have seemed to perish because they had been neglected. As it is, no small thing has been achieved: we blame not the physician, but the sick and their carelessness. Some walked uprightly before their trials and fell once the trials came. Others pursue every kind of wickedness and have never experienced any affliction. Still others, from earliest youth to their last breath, have been worn down by countless calamities. Let none of this trouble us or cast us down. If we were able, and obliged, to know the whole ordering of his providence and were still ignorant of these things, then we ought to be dejected and disturbed. But Paul, who shared in such great and unspeakable mysteries and ascended to the third heaven, grew dizzy before this abyss; he peered into the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, was simply struck with amazement, and at once drew back. Why then do we torment ourselves in vain, prying into what cannot be searched out and seeking what cannot be traced? A physician often prescribes things contrary to what seems good for us: he orders a chilled limb to be put under running water, and does many other such surprising things. Yet we do not argue with him. We have already convinced ourselves that he does this according to the principles of his art, and so we yield readily, even though he often makes mistakes. Shall we then pry into God, who is so far above us in every way, who is Wisdom itself, who never makes a mistake? Shall we simply trust the one from whom we ought to demand reasons, and demand accounts and reasons for his actions from the one whom alone we ought simply to trust, and chafe at our ignorance? How does this befit a devout soul? I beg and implore you, let us not come to such madness. In everything that perplexes us, let us say this: “Your judgments are a great abyss.” For it is itself part of God’s wisdom that we do not know everything clearly. If we obeyed God only when we knew the causes of what happens, our reward would not be great, and the matter would be no display of faith. But when we know none of these things and are still content to yield to all his commands, we greatly benefit our souls, leading them to genuine obedience and sincere faith. We must be convinced of one thing only: that everything God brings upon us is for our good. We should not go on to seek the manner of it, nor be vexed or dejected because we do not know it. For neither is it possible [?] … Colbert and Savile: “find” [?]. … After Morel: “nor we, having first persuaded ourselves”; [?]: “nor do we say, having first persuaded them”; Savile: “nor we (in the margin is added: [?] I seek) [?] having persuaded.” Shortly after, Savile and Colbert: “and into this”; [?]: “into this.”

…in prosperity and wealth, and even so they did not learn. But people now pry into far more than they did, for the things now set before us are far greater than those. So let the clear explanation of these things be left to him who knows all things before they come to be. 8. Still, for the sake of those who busy themselves too much with these questions, we may need to work out from what has already happened and is known to us some answer and consolation. If so, I say this: now that the kingdom has been revealed and the recompense of the age to come has been shown to us, the fact that the righteous suffer affliction while the wicked live in ease no longer even deserves inquiry. Since each person will receive what he deserves there, why should we be troubled by the good or evil that happens here? God trains those who are devoted to him with these labors, as he would noble athletes. But the weaker and slower, who cannot bear anything heavier, he first leads toward good works by encouragement. Often the opposite happens too: many of the righteous live in ease and honor, and many of the wicked in dishonor and the worst evils. In that case our earlier objection, which claims that the righteous suffer and the unrighteous live in luxury, is overturned by the facts themselves. If this point too must be resolved, I would say this: God does not usually manage our affairs in only one way. He is resourceful and cuts many roads to salvation for us. Many will not accept the teaching about the things to come and the resurrection. So he shows here, in brief, an image of the judgment, when he punishes the wicked and benefits the good. This happens completely at the judgment, but partially even here and now, so that those who have grown careless [?] about that distant time may at least become more reasonable through what is done in the present. If none of the wicked were ever punished and none of the good ever honored, many who disbelieve the teaching of the resurrection would flee virtue as a cause of evils and pursue wickedness as a source of good things. On the other hand, if everyone received what he deserved here, they would think the teaching of the judgment superfluous and false. So, so that this teaching is not disbelieved, and the great common crowd does not grow worse through contempt, he punishes many sinners even here and rewards some of those who do right. By not doing this to everyone, he confirms the teaching of the judgment. By punishing some even before the judgment, he wakes those who are sound asleep. When the wicked are punished, many are roused by fear of suffering the same. And because not everyone receives what he deserves here, they are forced to reason that this has been reserved for another time. Surely God, being just, would not have allowed so many to depart unpunished for their evil deeds, and so many others to be punished with countless terrors for their good deeds, unless he had prepared another state of existence for each of them. Therefore [?] … [?] “and slower” [?] in Savile [?].

…and when they come to their senses, they do no less than these. I do not mean what they do while the demon has hold of them, but what they do afterward, once that frenzy has stopped. For they gorge themselves, steal, get drunk, and do things far more shameful than these. Think of how a judge deals with criminals. Most of them he leaves to live for a long time in prison, so that they often end their lives there. But when he wishes to warn the many, he takes one or two of them, sits on his high tribunal with everyone standing around, and orders the condemned man to be led to his death. He does not need all the wicked in order to make the rest afraid. In the same way God, when he wishes to bring us to our senses, does not need all the wicked. He takes some of them whom he knows to be incorrigible, and displays his power and his wrath, and achieves much by this. In this way he calls the wicked to turn from their wickedness, if they are willing; he makes the good more attentive; he displays his own patience; and, as I have already said, he makes the teaching about the resurrection clear to all. “What then,” someone says, “of those who are raised in calamity throughout their early childhood and die before they come to tell good from evil?” Tell me, what terrible thing do they suffer? They do not yet have any awareness of what they suffer, and have not learned to grieve or to rejoice. But I do not answer this question in this way only. I also say that parents, brothers, and relatives have been brought to their senses by such calamities. And this is no small gain: one person suffers no real wrong, and from that same event another person benefits greatly. It is also likely that there is some other reason that cannot be spoken, evident only to the one who made us. 9. One question still remains: why did those who walked uprightly before their trials fall after them? Who truly knows which people walk uprightly, except the one who fashioned our hearts one by one and understands all our works? Many who seem good are often worse than anyone. This has been shown even in the present life, though only in some cases, when some crisis or necessity arose. But the one who tests hearts and minds, who is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, who pierces to the division of soul and body, of joints and marrow, and who discerns thoughts and intentions, will sit and judge us. Then, at that time, you will see not just a few out of many but all such people exposed. Sheep’s clothing will not be able to hide the wolf, nor whitewash the filth inside a tomb. For no creature is hidden before the one who judges then; all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes. Paul made this clear when he said to the Corinthians: “Therefore do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts.” But let us leave the hypocrites and turn our discussion to those who live rightly. How do we know whether, though they have achieved everything else, they have neglected the chief of all good things, humility? For this reason God let them fall, so that they might learn that it was not by their own power [?] … [?] of beasts hard to catch [?]; Savile in the text, and [?].

…this demon. That is why I never cease to be astonished at you and to admire you. Though you were allotted such an adversary, you did not fall or give yourself up, but remained unbending, and nothing overturned you from any side. 10. I am not saying this to flatter you; you have truly reaped the greatest benefits from this affliction. To show this, bear with me while I speak frankly, for I could not prove it any other way. You surely know and remember your former way of life, I mean before this trial. Examine it carefully and set it beside your present way of life since the trial, and then you will see how great a gain this struggle has brought you. Now your fasts and night vigils, your zeal for reading, and your perseverance in prayer have greatly increased, and you have achieved self-restraint [?] and humility to an extraordinary degree. Before, you paid no attention to books, and all your care and labor went into tending the plants in the garden. At that time I used to hear many people mocking you for your arrogance, and blaming it on the distinction of your family, your father’s renown, and your upbringing in great wealth. And your sluggishness at the night vigils you yourself know well. Often, when the others rose promptly late in the night [?], you stayed fast asleep and were annoyed with those who woke you. But now all that is gone and has changed for the better, ever since you took up this battle and this war. You may ask me why God did not allow this demon to attack you while you lived in luxury and were infatuated with the things of the world. I would answer that this too was part of his care. He knew that the demon would find you easy to overcome at that time and would quickly destroy you. That is why he did not call you to this contest as soon as you entered the monastic life. He let you train and wait a long time, and only when you had become very steadfast did he draw you into this toilsome arena. Will you still bring up people who live in the world, and point to your servant? For I think you are hinting at him when you say that many men of the world who fell into this illness obtained a very quick and complete [?] … Savile and Colbert: “into countless thoughts.” BY THE SAME AUTHOR, TO STAGIRIUS, AND THAT DEPRESSION IS WORSE EVEN THAN A DEMON. SECOND DISCOURSE. 1. Let this be what we have to say about God’s providence: it is not because he turns away from you or hates you, but because he loves you greatly, that he trains you in this way. But you also said that you suffer intensely in another way: the demon often tries to persuade you to destroy yourself in the sea or over a cliff, or to end your present life in some other such way. So I wish to say a little about these thoughts too. For this counsel comes not from him alone, but also from your depression [?] … having extinguished [?], and to take away their possessions, and could slaughter their owners with great ease [?]

In the same way this one too spreads despondency in place of night and darkness and tries to steal away every thought that makes for safety, so that he may catch the soul deserted and helpless and wound it with countless blows. But when someone scatters this darkness by hope in God, takes refuge in the Sun of righteousness and hurries to let those rays into his own soul, he will shift the turmoil from his own thoughts onto the robber. For people who commit such crimes tremble, grow dizzy and are thrown into confusion when someone exposes them and shows a light. “And how,” you ask, “could anyone be rid of this pain without first being rid of the demon that stirs it up?” It is not the demon that stirs up despondency. Rather, despondency makes the demon strong and suggests the evil thoughts. Blessed Paul would bear us witness here. It was not some demon but too much of this sorrow that he feared when he wrote to the Corinthians to spare from then on the man who had sinned, in the matter in which he had sinned: “Lest such a one,” he says, “be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.” If you like, let us suppose for argument's sake that the demon is pressing on you but despondency has been driven out of your soul. What harm will there be then? What could he do by himself to hurt us, in small things or great? But despondency could do many terrible things even without him. We shall find that most of those who have hanged themselves, or died by the sword, or drowned themselves in rivers, or killed themselves in some other way, were driven to these violent deaths by despondency. And if some of them were also possessed by demons, their destruction too must be blamed not on the demon but on the tyranny and violence of despondency. “And how is it possible,” you ask, “not to be despondent?” It is possible if you stand apart from what most people think about the matter and set your mind on things above. As things are, because most people think the thing terrible, it seems so to you too. But if you are willing to free yourself from vain and mistaken prejudice and look closely at the thing in itself, you will find that it gives no occasion for despondency, as we have already shown many times. As for your companions of the same age (for I suppose it is seeing their cheerfulness and their freedom of speech with the brothers that confounds you and casts you down), I would say this. If they lived in self-control and good order and the rest of the philosophic life while you spent all your time in brothels, at dice and in revels, your excuse for despondency would make sense. But if you still walk the same road as they do, what is it that grieves you? If I were speaking to someone else, one of those who are easily puffed up, I would have kept silent about what I am now going to say to you. But I am quite confident that, however much anyone praises and admires you, you will never give up your modesty but will still rank yourself among the last. So I will say everything and hold nothing back. I hear that your piety has advanced so far that you no longer compete with those youths but with great and admirable men. They say you fall short of them in nothing, not in fasting (for how, with water [?] [Note: So Savile and the Colbert manuscript; Morel reads “is thought to be, it seems so to you too.”]

[?] So when petty men insult you, bearing the insult earns praise; but when the most wicked of all does this very thing, must the man who has nobly borne his madness hide himself in shame, as though he had done something blameworthy? What could be more absurd than this contradiction? If, after getting up from that fall, you had been led to do or say something improper, I myself would not have stopped you from beating your breast and grieving over it. But if you bear everything with thanksgiving and turn at once to prayer, what is it that causes the shame? Perhaps it is the reproaches of others that hurt. But what could deserve more reproach than these people, who cannot even rightly know what ought to be reproached? These are truly the mad and the demon-possessed. They have not learned to see things as they really are; they blame what deserves praise and move what deserves reproach into the ranks of the praised. People sick with delirium say many cruel things to those around them, yet the hearers do not consider themselves insulted. So do not you either, when you hear those deranged people, consider the thing a disgrace and an insult, or you may truly make yourself worthy of reproach by provoking God. For when you consider as a reproach what God sends for discipline and benefit, see where the [?] ends

3. If you wish to see the people who truly deserve shame and reproach, I will try to point out to you in words a few out of many. Look at those who are infatuated with the beauty of women; those who are mad for money; those who are in love with power and glory and will do and suffer anything for them; those who waste away with envy; those who plot against people who have done them no wrong; those who are simply melancholy; those who are forever raging over the vanities of life. These things and things like them are the works of madness and deserve punishment; these deserve reproach, shame and ridicule. But if someone troubled by a demon still shows great philosophy in his life, he would deserve not only to escape reproach but to be admired and crowned by everyone, since he runs such a laborious race in such fetters and climbs the steep and rough road of virtue. Somehow, though, I almost passed over another way in which you have the advantage over the brothers: if you have committed any fault, you can easily strip off these sins as well through this affliction. This became clear to us from what I discussed earlier, when I spoke about Lazarus and about the man among the Corinthians who had committed fornication. “But I am afraid for my father,” you say. “Even if I can bear my own troubles calmly, how shall we easily bear his calamities and his fury, if he should ever notice any of this?” So far he has not noticed. And it shows great faintheartedness to reap despondency already, and beat one's breast, over things that will happen at some later time, or will not happen at all. How is it clear to us that he will notice? But let it be clear, rather, and let it be granted, if you like, that he will notice and will do terrible things. I commend you for grieving [?] [Note: … reads “should display”; a little later Savile and the Colbert manuscript read “with so many”.]

[?] will wish you to box [?] this contest of yours [?] that leads to life. And that it is impossible ever to walk through the [?] of [?] the earth in spaciousness is surely clear to everyone. I myself have nothing precise to say about these things, nor can I make declarations about the future. This much, however, I know clearly, and I ask you to be convinced of it too: whichever of these things happens, it will be to our advantage. And if you are of this mind, you will quickly beat off even the crowning point of these troubles, as you call it.

Besides this, we must also bear in mind that the time for prizes and crowns is the age to come, while the time for wrestling and sweat is the present. Blessed Paul wished to make this clear to us when he said: “So I run, not aimlessly; so I box, not as one beating the air; but I bruise my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.” And when he reached the end, he uttered that blessed saying: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness.” He was showing that our whole life must be one of struggle and toil, if we are to enjoy the eternal rest and its countless good things. If someone wants to take it easy and enjoy the pleasures of this world and also the rewards stored up there for those who labor, he deceives and cheats himself. With athletes, the one who looks for relaxation at the time of the contests earns himself shame and disgrace for all time, while the one who nobly bears every toil in the stadium reaps crowns, glory and praise from the spectators, both during the contests and after they are over. So it is with us too. The one who makes the time of labor a time of relaxation will wail and gnash his teeth when he ought to be resting in that ageless repose, and will suffer the worst of evils. But the one who willingly bears afflictions here will be illustrious both here and there, glorious with a glory that is true and immortal. In worldly affairs, the man who confuses the right timing of things will lose everything set before him and surround himself with countless misfortunes. Much more will this happen in spiritual matters to the man who does not know the order of the seasons. Christ said, “In the world you will have affliction.” Blessed Paul said, “And all who wish to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted,” meaning not only persecutions from men but also the plots of demons. Job said, “The life of man on earth is a trial.” Why then are you vexed at being afflicted in the season of hardship? We would have reason to grieve if we made the time that Christ foretold would be a time of affliction into a season of luxury and rest; if we lay back at our ease in the very time when we were commanded to struggle and toil; if we walked the broad road when he commanded the narrow one. Then punishment in those ages would follow for us of necessity. “What then would one say,” you ask, “about those who walk in spaciousness here and will also rest there?” And who is this? For I trust only the word of Christ, who says, “Narrow and hard is the way [Note: The Colbert manuscript and Savile read “besides this”; Morel reads “besides this” in a different case. The Colbert manuscript and Savile read “and just as with”. [?] in the Colbert manuscript: “in the last”.]

[?] shut up in that narrow space, what do you think he went through at the crash of the thunder and the noise of the rains? The deep below was bursting up, and the deep above was pouring down, and he sat inside alone with his sons. Even if he could be confident about the outcome, the violence of what was happening must have half killed him with fear beforehand. We have houses set firmly on the ground and live in cities, yet when we see a little more rain fall than usual we lose heart and shrink back. What would he not have suffered, alone inside, thinking of that most dreadful deep and of all the different kinds of creatures that were drowning? It is enough to strike the soul with terror when a single city, or even a single house, is flooded and covered by the waves. But when the whole inhabited world suffered this, there are no words to say what state it put him in, as he was carried about in the midst of the surge. For that whole year, then, he was gripped by such great fear. And when at last the flood stopped, his fear eased, but his despondency grew. When he peered out of the ark, another storm no less than the first took its place, as he saw the vast desolation, that violent death, the bodies of the slain smeared with slime and mud, and everyone together, men and asses and the meaner kinds of animals, buried in a single most pitiful grave. Even if those who suffered this were great sinners, Noah was still a human being and felt something for his own kind. Ezekiel too, though he was righteous and knew that the Israelites were the most wicked of all, felt this common emotion and wept when he saw them being slaughtered and falling. And this was in spite of God having revealed their whole impiety to him in advance, and having let him see it with his own eyes, precisely so that he might bear the calamity bravely when he saw them punished. Yet even with such consolation prepared for him beforehand, he was overcome, and fell down and cried out, “Alas, Lord, are you wiping out the remnant of Israel?” And this happened to him not just once but again, when he saw Jechoniah being killed. So Noah too, even if he knew of countless evils on their part, was no braver than this prophet or than Moses. Moses too often felt the same as the prophet: when he saw the people sinning and they had to be punished, he grieved and was in more pain than those who were being punished. In Noah's case the calamity was even harsher, for that was the only death of its kind. He was beset, then, by so many evils: his loneliness, his sympathy for his own kind, the multitude of the dead, the manner of their end, the desolation of the earth. And while his despondency was rising on every side and at its height, his son's insult was immediately added: an unbearable thing, full of great shame and great pain. For just as reproaches from friends are harder to bear than those from enemies, reproaches from one's children are more unbearable still. For when the one he begot, whom he raised, whom he brought up, for whom he endured many toils, labors and anxieties, [turns out to be] more insulting than anyone [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “he pitied, and more”; Savile reads “had to, he pitied, and grieved more and was in pain”.]

[?] traveling a road, and striving not to turn aside even a little over so great a distance, while many in the meantime hindered him? [?] Having asked how far he was forced to travel, we heard [?] that it was a count of thirty-five days. And why do I say many? Rather the whole [?], and the road was such, from the ends of the earth to the ends, full of crags, thorns, wild beasts, drought, plague, frost and evildoers. It would be easier to walk a well-worn path continually in the depth of night than to walk the road of virtue in those times, so many were there who forcibly tried to turn his steps [?] aside. When everyone may do whatever they like, and only one man walks the opposite way, how will he be able to reach the end when all are pushing him back and repelling him? How hard it is to do right while living among many is shown by those who have taken to the deserts now, even at a time when, by the grace of God, good living can be seen spread everywhere, along with no small concord and mutual affection. But back then there was none of this; everyone was more savage toward him than wild beasts. 6. What could be more painful than this life? What could be more wretched than this existence? I promised to show that he was no better off than those who carry burdens all the time and never get a breath. But the argument has done much more: it has shown us that he was not only no better off but far more heavily burdened than they are. Many people think that Abraham spent his whole life in good cheer, and so they usually compare him with those who prosper and flourish on every side. Come then, let us examine what happened to him. To me this man [seems] far more than both Noah and Abel — but rather I will say nothing until the examination of the facts casts its vote for us. Of what happened to him in Persia, and of any grief he had up to the age of seventy, no one could know clearly. For blessed Moses did not write the history of that period for us; he left out that whole stage of life and began his account from what came afterward. But it was likely that he too suffered the same things as Noah, since he alone wished to be godly among so many impious barbarians. This is not as obscure as the rest; even the very foolish could easily guess it. Still, let these things be set aside for now. Let us begin our account with his emigration, first examining how far the land of the Chaldeans is from Palestine, what the roads were like, how people's dealings with one another were arranged, and what their way of life was. Because that righteous man obeyed readily, do not now think the thing was easy. And because Moses told what happened concisely and briefly, do not think the deed matched the brevity of the words. Saying and narrating these things is easy, but doing them is not equally easy; it is very hard. The length of the road, and how far apart these places are, could be told precisely by those who have come to us from there, if indeed there are any [Note: Savile and Morel read “famine” for “plague”. [?]]

[?] he roamed everywhere in his mind and took great turmoil into his soul. He could not come to rest anywhere in his reasoning; he had many suspicions and was forced to worry. He probably expected to reach the very ends of the inhabited world, even the Ocean itself. So even if he did not travel over the whole earth, he endured the anxiety of such a great journey. For he had not prepared his soul as one who would go only as far as Palestine, but as one who would follow anywhere, even if he were commanded to go beyond the inhabited world, even to the islands outside it. And if the vagueness of the command led him to expect the opposite as well, that too was hard. For someone who is about to endure something burdensome, it is much easier to know clearly what he will undergo and what to prepare for, than to wander everywhere in his thoughts, now expecting good things, now the opposite, unable to be confident about any of them, but in both alike

7. That was before he came to the promised land. But when at last he reached Palestine and expected to rest at last, he found a greater storm in the harbor itself. This is no small cause of pain; it is the most unbearable of all. Someone thinks he is free and has come to the end of it, and has set aside every care and worry, and then he finds another round of difficulties starting all over again. The man who is still prepared for hardships would bear their onset more easily. But the man who has relaxed and released his thoughts from their cares is doubly troubled if something like what happened before happens again. He becomes easy to overpower, both because it is unexpected and because all his effort and preparation have been dissolved. What then was the storm? A famine so severe seized Palestine at that time that it immediately drove him out of there and brought him down to Egypt. He went there to find relief from the trouble, but fell into a misfortune harsher than the famine and was forced to risk his very life. He came to be in such fear that he chose what is the most unbearable thing of all for anyone: the violation of his own wife. [?] He was reduced to such necessity that he even lent himself to the pretense. What could be more pitiable than that? What state of soul do you think he was in when he was forced to give his wife advice like this? “I know that you are a beautiful woman. So when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife,’ and they will kill me but keep you alive. So say, ‘I am his sister,’ so that it may go well with me because of you, and my soul may live [?] for your sake.” These were the words spoken by the man who for God's sake had left his country, his household, his friends, his relatives and everything else at home, and who had endured such hardship and so much toil over that long time on the journey. And yet he said nothing like “God has abandoned me, has turned away, has cast me out of his providence.” Instead he bore everything nobly and faithfully. He, of all people the one who ought to have been angry when his wife was being violated, under the great pressure did everything so that the outrage might not even come to light. Words cannot express how much despondency and pain this brings, but those who [?] know [Note: Morel reads “find”. The same [?] reads “nor will he change”.]

…if it happened that after the marriage a first year passed, then a second, or even a third, the despondency grows stronger and the better hopes grow weaker. When still more time is added, those hopes finally vanish altogether, and despondency takes hold of the soul, casting a shadow over every pleasure and letting him feel none of them. So even if none of all these troubles had befallen him, and everything had gone as he wished, the despondency of childlessness, hanging over everything that happened, would have been enough to darken and destroy all his cheerfulness. For God's promise came in extreme old age, when nature had already been given up for lost; and through the whole long time before that he went on grieving and beating his breast, and the more he saw his wealth increase, the more he mourned, since there was no one to inherit it. What do you suppose he felt when he heard: "Your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own, and they will enslave them and mistreat them and humble them for four hundred years"? And his wife, who first told him to take her maidservant, and then, once he had taken her, accused and blamed him, called on God against him, and forced him to drive out the woman who had shared his bed and was about to bear him a child: whom would that not have cast into the deepest despondency? If these things seem small to anyone now, let him consider that whole households have been overturned on their account, and let him admire the righteous man. For though he bore it nobly out of fear of God, he was still a man, and all these things stung and pained him. Then the servant girl comes back to her master's house and bears him the illegitimate son, and Abraham becomes a father after all that long time. The event brought some pleasure, but greater despondency. For the illegitimate son reminded him of the legitimate one and stirred up a greater longing for him. He thought the words "This one will not be your heir, but one who will come from your own body" were spoken about Ishmael, for nothing had yet been said about Sarah. And when at last he received a clearer promise about Isaac and a time was fixed for the birth, before he could again take pleasure in these hopes, the calamities of the Sodomites poured a thick mist of despondency over him. That this event troubled the righteous man in no ordinary way is plain to everyone from his very words and from the plea he made to God on their behalf. And when he saw that most dreadful rain come down, and everything suddenly turned to dust and ashes, he was no longer himself. For if we lose our wits and collapse from despondency and fear when we see houses burning far off, what would he not have suffered when he saw whole cities and regions with their inhabitants burned up, and not by ordinary fire but by a strange and terrible one? Do you not think the sufferings of the righteous man resemble the endless succession of waves on the sea? Just as there the next waves rise to a crest before the first have died away, so it went all through the life of this righteous man. For while the evils in Sodom were still at their height, the king of Gerar attempted the same outrage against Sarah that Pharaoh had dared, and once again his wife was forced to play that pitiable pretence… [?] (Morel: "what do you think"; Savile: "what then do you think".)

…"will provide himself a sheep for a whole burnt offering, my child." How full of tenderness do you think these words are? But each received honour, hearing, "Enter into the jo[?]": he held his pain down and suppressed it, and with [?] "…of your Lord." What then of Isaac? A journey [?] he did everything with as much eagerness as men who are held back by none of these hindrances. So he sacrificed him (for he did sacrifice him, in his willingness) and handed him back safe and sound to his mother. But she, once she had him back, died before she had enjoyed her son to the full. This too grieved Abraham not a little. Though she had lived with him a long time, nothing could persuade him to bear the loss more easily. In fact this very thing made his despondency greater, for those who have lived with us a long time and given us much proof of their friendship and virtue are the ones we miss most of all. That this is so the patriarch himself showed by mourning and lamenting her. And what should one say of his worries over his son, over his son's wife, over his son's brothers, and over everything else? If anyone wished to examine them closely, he would see that the righteous man's life was far more painful than has been shown here, and full of more cares. For Scripture tells only the main points and leaves us to consider all the rest, everything likely to happen every day in a household with a crowd of servants, husband and wife and children, and the management of many affairs. "Yes," someone says, "but in each of these troubles he found the greatest consolation in enduring them all for God's sake." Then let this console you now as well, for the one who allowed this trial to come upon you is none other than God. If those wicked demons would not have dared to leap upon the swine unless he had permitted it then, much less would they dare to attack your precious soul. So just as bearing everything nobly and with thanksgiving brought him a great reward, it will bring you one too, provided only that you do not chafe or grow indignant, but give thanks for everything to the God who loves humankind. Blessed Job too suffered what he suffered by God's permission, yet what won him his crowns was not the suffering alone but his standing firm and noble against every terror. And we all admire him, not because the devil stripped him of everything, but because in all these things he did not sin, not even with his lips.

10. Since I have mentioned Job, I would have liked to set out in my discourse his long laments and the severity of his sufferings; but so as not to make this too long, I return to Isaac. If you wish to learn Job's story in detail, take his book in hand and look down into the abyss of his misfortunes, and you will find much consolation for your own. For though the righteous man was far better than we are, he also fought against a far greater force, since the Evil One then blew more violently against him. But achievements are judged not by the size of the trials but by the strength with which one acts. So even if this present contest of yours is smaller, that can do you no harm with regard to the crowns. For the one who brought the two talents received no less than the one who produced five. Why? Because even if the income… (Savile: "since the one who [brought] the two talents".)

…they were forced; but the wicked one, who made their life miserable and unbearable (Rebekah herself says this), they kept with them all the time. And when the other fled, the one who had always been brought up at home (for he was a plain man, dwelling at home) and who mostly stayed in the house with his mother, how much must Rebekah have grieved and lamented, constantly remembering her son and seeing her husband in no better state than the dead, because of his age and his illness? And how much grief must the old man have suffered with his household, forced as he was to lament his wife's misfortunes as well? When she was about to die, what did she not say, what words did she not utter, enough to melt a stone, as she did not see her son standing beside her and weeping, closing her eyes, shutting her mouth, laying out her body, and attending to everything else, things that parents think more bitter than death itself to be without? And Isaac, seeing her breathe her last in this way, what kind of soul he had, both then and after her…

11. Such, then, has the man who seemed more cheerful than many turned out to be. As for Jacob's life, Jacob's own statement is enough to show it even without examination. For when he was talking with Pharaoh he said: "Few and evil have been my days, and they have not reached the days of my fathers"; that is, I have lived a shorter and more wretched life. But even apart from that statement, his misfortunes are so well known that not even ordinary people are ignorant of them. His grandfather, though he set out on a long journey, did so at God's command, and this brought him the greatest consolation; but Jacob was fleeing a brother who was plotting against him and bent on murdering him. Abraham never lamented over the supply of necessities, while Jacob thought it something to be content with and to pray for merely to have bread and clothing. He came through safely, was rid of the hardships of the road and reached his own kinsmen, and then the man who had been raised in such plenty was forced to serve as a slave. You know that slavery is bitter everywhere; but when someone is forced to endure the lot of a servant among his equals, and that without ever having experienced such a thing, having spent all his early life in freedom and comfort, the misery becomes unbearable. Yet he bore it all nobly. You hear him describing his hardships as a shepherd and saying: "I myself made good what was stolen by day and what was stolen by night; I was scorched by the heat of the day and the frost of the night, and sleep fled from my eyes. Twenty years I have had of this." These were the sufferings of the man who had lived the plain life and always dwelt at home. And after so many labours and losses and all that long time, he endured the bitter deception over his wife. Even if he had not served the seven years, even if he had suffered none of the things he complained of to his father-in-law, even if he had not loved the girl, the mere fact that the better woman was promised to him and the lesser one given in her place: how much despondency, how much turmoil, how much insult did it cause that blessed man then? Anyone else would not easily have… (Savile: "which was enough even to melt a stone".) [?] (Colbert: "is forced".)

…but his whole life, from that day on which, as he was about to receive the blessings, he had all but died of fear beforehand, was a web of misfortunes and plots. Such fear gripped him then that even after the meeting, though his brother treated him kindly and generously, he did not take heart or lay aside his anxiety. When his brother urged him to travel on with him, he begged off and contrived his withdrawal as though he were about to escape some wild beast, saying: "My lord knows that the children are frail, and the sheep and cattle with me are giving birth; if I drive them too hard, all the livestock will die in a single day. Let my lord go on ahead of his servant, and I will make my way along the road at a leisurely pace, keeping to the pace of the journey before me and of my children, until I come to my lord at Seir." And having breathed a little after those dangers, he fell again into another, much worse one.

For when his daughter was carried off, at first he grieved over the outrage done to the girl. But when the king's son was trying to make amends for what had happened by promising to take her as his lawful wife, and Jacob had approved the plan, Levi and his brothers broke the agreement, destroyed the city with all its men, and threw their father into such terror that he had to move away from there, because everyone had become hostile to him. For Jacob, it says, said to Simeon and Levi: "You have made me hateful, so that I am odious to all who live in the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites; and I am few in number, and they will gather against me and cut me down, and I shall be destroyed, I and my house." And indeed the neighbours would have slaughtered them all, had not God's love for humankind restrained their anger and put an end to those evils: "For a terror from God," it says, "fell upon all the cities around them, and they did not pursue the sons of Israel." What then? Once he was rid of these things, did he breathe again? No: that was when the crowning evil came upon him, the death of the woman he loved, a death both untimely and violent. "For Rachel gave birth," it says, "and had hard labour. And as she was in hard labour, the midwife said to her, 'Take heart, for this one too is a son for you.' And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she named him Son of my pain." And while the mourning was still at its height, Reuben added to his despondency by defiling his father's bed. He took this so hard that even on his deathbed he cursed his son, at the very time when parents feel most tenderly toward their children, and though this was the firstborn of all the rest, which counts for not a little where love is concerned. Yet the force of his despondency thrust all this aside, and he called him and said: "Reuben, my firstborn, my strength and the first of my children, hard to bear, hard and headstrong: you have run riot; like water, do not boil over. For you went up to your father's bed; then you defiled the couch you climbed onto." And when the son of his beloved wife had grown up, and he expected to find in him consolation for his grief over her, then all kinds of misfortunes were contrived for him through this son… (Savile and Colbert: "to have cursed"; Morel: "to curse".)

[?] …I am bereaved. He was so overwhelmed by his many evils that even as his heart was torn and his sons were taken from him one by one, he endured everything because the greater evils outweighed it. For he felt greater despondency over these sons than over Joseph. A misfortune that holds no hope of remedy, though it brings us intense despondency, nevertheless drives it out quickly by casting the mind into despair; but one still hanging in the balance gives the soul no rest, for the uncertainty of the future keeps intensifying and renewing our anguish. One can learn this well from blessed David, who lamented his child while it was still alive, but released himself from mourning once it had died. When his servants were puzzled and asked him the reason, he gave the very reasoning I am giving now. So it was natural that Jacob too was more fearful and trembled more for these sons. The longed-for sight of Joseph did give him cheer afterwards. But what was the gain? Just as limbs badly burned by fire are not helped even if one cools them countless times, so too nothing could restore his soul, which had been filled with pain and badly burned by the flame of despondency, especially since his senses were likely no longer sharp. This is what Barzillai said when he declined David's invitation: "How many days of the years of my life are left to me, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am eighty years old today; can I tell good from bad? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks, or hear the voices of men and women singing? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?" But why must we infer these things from others, when we can hear from the sufferer himself? For after he had seen his son, when Pharaoh asked him about his life, he said: "Few and evil have been my days, and they have not reached the days of my fathers." So vivid did he always keep the memory of what had happened in his soul.

12. But this illustrious and glorious son, Joseph: whom did he not surpass in misfortunes? His father had only one brother plotting against him, but Joseph had many more. Jacob was raised through all his early years in plenty and great ease, while Joseph, in a foreign land and still a child, was forced to bear the hardships of the road. Jacob had a mother at hand to ease the danger of the plot, while Joseph, still young and at the age when he most needed a mother, was left without that help. Besides this, Esau grieved Jacob only with threats, but these brothers carried their plot into action, and even before the plot they kept envying and slandering him. What could be harder than to have the people you live with as constant enemies? "For they brought an evil report against him; and seeing that their father loved him more than all his other sons, they hated him and could not speak a peaceable word to him." For neither [?] to the merchants… [?] …or of Joseph. [?] quickly; Morel: "but nevertheless quickly" [?] …David, who when [?] alive… [?] …of the king had been released, he himself still remained inside. But do not tell me about the jailer's kindness; examine Joseph's words, and you will see the anguish of his

soul. For after interpreting the dream he said to the cupbearer: "But remember me yourself when things go well with you, and show me kindness: mention me to Pharaoh and get me out of this stronghold. For I was stolen away from the land of the Hebrews, and here too I have done nothing, yet they threw me into this dungeon." Even if he bore imprisonment with ease, living among such men, grave robbers, thieves, parricides, adulterers, murderers (for the place was full of all these and their like), weighed on him more heavily than anything. And not only did this grieve and oppress him, but also seeing many men wasting away there for nothing and in vain. Yet the slave, and this is the very thing you are lamenting now, was set free from his chains, while the free man stayed on in his misery. And if anyone mentions his rule, he will again be speaking to me of a swarm of cares, sleepless nights and countless affairs, all of which, for those who embrace a quiet and untroubled life, are not very… (Colbert and Savile: "to be removed".)

BY THE SAME, TO STAGIRIUS, ON DESPONDENCY. THIRD DISCOURSE.

1. What has been said is enough to quench the flame of despondency and to persuade the soul to be more at ease. But so that the consolation may be more than enough, I have decided to add this discourse as well, first asking you this. Tell me: if someone summoned you to a kingdom on earth, and before entering the city and putting on the crown you had to stay at an inn full of mud and smoke, the noise of travellers, the disturbance of robbers, cramped quarters and great discomfort, would you turn back because of those hardships? Or would you not despise them all as nothing? How then is it not absurd that a man about to rule the earth should shrink from none of the difficulties that come his way, exulting in his hopes of the kingdom, while one bound for heaven collapses and is thrown into turmoil by each of the hardships that befall us in this lodging? For the condition of this life is no different from a lodging-house and a stay at an inn. The saints, wishing to show this, called themselves strangers and sojourners, teaching us by these words to laugh at both the good things and the painful things of the present life, and, set free from the earth, to bind ourselves wholly to heaven.

Come, then, let us turn to the saints themselves, moving our discourse from Joseph to Moses. This man, the meekest of all on earth, was born at a time when his people were faring badly, and estranged [?]… (he said). [?] …to the same, still on despondency; Savile: "to the same Stagirius, discourse 3". Margin: "difficulties".

…to enjoy [?] the consolation that came from that act of vengeance? A second day had not even come before a sorrow harsher than the first took its place in that blessed man, and a fear so great that it drove him out of all Egypt. It is a terrible thing to be spoken ill of by anyone at all. But when the one doing it is someone who has been helped, and who reproaches you with the help you gave him and throws it in your face ("Do you mean to kill me," he says, "as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?"), then, yes, then the insult becomes unbearable. It could even choke the one who is insulted, so much anger does it bring along with the dejection. In Moses' case there was also a third thing besides these: fear of the king. This fear so overpowered the righteous man's soul that it drove him out of the whole country. So the king's son becomes a fugitive. If anyone counts him blessed because he was brought up in the palace, let him now remember that abundance, and he will see that it gave the righteous man grounds for countless sorrows and hardships. Consider a man raised in a private household, who has endured many labors and many journeys abroad and hardships, and then has to bear long wanderings and suffer the troubles of a foreign land. Now consider a man who never had even a brief taste of such things and spent all his time in luxury, and then suffers the very same thing. Their case is not the same. The second will feel exile far more harshly than the first, if he should ever be reduced to that necessity. This is exactly what happened to Moses then. Once he became a fugitive, he lodged with an idolater and a foreigner. This too was no small cause for dejection: to be the guest, for so long, of a man who was a priest of demons. He was entrusted with the care of that man's flocks, and so he spent forty years.
