If anyone thinks this was nothing terrible, let us look at people who go abroad and hide, not out of fear and dread, but who willingly leave home for a little while. See how restless they are, how they chafe, how many good things they would give for their return. But when fear is present too, and a life of hardship, and these burdensome and oppressive things seem lighter than the sweetest return [?], then look at how many-sided the misfortune is. Do not simply hear the words "he was shepherding." Remember now the words of Jacob, with which he complained to his father-in-law: "I made good from my own stock what was stolen by day and what was stolen by night. By day I was scorched by the heat, and by night by the frost, and sleep fled from my eyes." All these things were likely to happen to Moses as well, for more years and with greater severity, since that country was more desolate than the other. If Moses did not complain of these things, [?] it is because that blessed Jacob would not have spoken either if he had not been in great distress, forced into these words by his father-in-law's ingratitude. A foreign land is enough in itself to humble a man, even one who is abroad only out of some need. "As a bird," it says, "when it flies out of its nest, so a man is enslaved when he is exiled from his own." [?]

…and he was held in a greater darkness. He feared not only the Egyptians, as the rest of the Israelites did, but these Israelites as well as the Egyptians. Both now regarded him as a deceiver and a pretender: the Egyptians with mockery and gloating, the Israelites with bitterness and dejection. But why should we judge the man's dejection by these things, when we can learn all his anguish from the voice that came from above? He was silent and did not dare even to open his lips, yet God says to him, "Why do you cry out to me?" By this one phrase God shows us the turmoil in his soul.

3. When this fear too had passed, greater troubles arose again. Throughout the whole journey, the people he was leading, who had enjoyed countless benefits through him, treated him more harshly than the Egyptians and Pharaoh had. First they pressed hard on him, throttling him and demanding the meat of Egypt. They were ungrateful for what they had and longed for what they had before, which was the hardest thing of all. What could he have suffered that was worse, if he had been put in command of raving lunatics? Yet that blessed man bore all this nobly. If he had not loved them tenderly, the trouble would have been bearable, and it would have pained him only because of what was done to him. But as it was, he felt more for them than parents do, and this very care gave him another, unavoidable cause of dejection: their perversity and corruption. Being insulted did not sting him as much as the fact that they were the ones insulting him. It was a terrible thing to be ungrateful before that marvelous food was provided. But even in the midst of the miracles they displayed their wickedness, their disobedience and their greed in the gathering. And when they had gone a little further, they grumbled again and again found fault with God's benefits. At each of these offenses that blessed man beat his breast and was more dejected than the sinners themselves. When they made the calf, they played and reveled, while Moses was the one mourning and grieving and calling down that terrible curse on himself. And nothing at all could persuade him to give up his compassion for them. So, seeing those he loved so much always going from bad to worse, with how much grief, with how many tears must he have lived! A man with one son could not go on living if he saw that son turn to vice, even if he himself happened to be the worst of all men. What then of one who had so many tens of thousands in place of children, or rather loved them more than children? For no father would pray to perish together with his child when he himself had done no wrong, as Moses did. What do you think a man with so many children, who hated evil and loved good, suffered when he saw them all run down the cliff of vice, as if at some signal? If the dizziness of that dejection had not darkened him badly and overturned his soul from its foundations, he would not have hurled the tablets from his hands and broken them. Yet he quickly healed the disaster. By doing what, tell me? The way he healed it, though it brought comfort for what had happened, was itself full of many tears. And no one was so stony as to feel nothing…

…these words did not end his compassion for them, as is clear to us from what he did afterward. After the affair of the spies they tried to kill him and pelted him with stones. Yet when he had escaped their hands, he turned again to prayer for them and begged God to be merciful to those who wanted to kill him. So much stronger than natural affection was the love that dwelt in him. The spies died, and while the mourning was at its height, before any time had passed, they again wove other causes of dejection for him. First they would not listen when he forbade them to fight, and then they were cut down by the Amalekites. Even before this war they had been badly wasted by cholera and gluttony. "For he killed," it says, "among the most of them, while the food was still in their mouths." He saw that great death there, and before his dejection over it had ended, he was struck by another grief. He was brought to such straits that he prayed for these beloved and dearest people to end their lives by a strange and unheard-of death. So some were burned when fire suddenly broke out, and others were swallowed when a chasm opened. Those who suffered this were not a few who could easily be counted, but more than fifteen thousand men. After this, how were their relatives and friends likely to feel toward Moses? And how did Moses himself feel? He saw children orphaned and wives widowed by this disaster. He saw his sister and his brother die, and his brother's sons burned for some transgression. Each of these things is enough to afflict a soul that has suffered nothing, let alone one already worn down by so many evils. When they had defeated the Canaanite and were going round by a long road, the Jews grumbled again, and again they perished. This time it was not by disease, as before, nor by fire and chasm, as earlier, but by the bites of venomous snakes. These would have destroyed them all if Moses had not again come forward and pleaded with God. When they had been delivered from this destruction and had escaped the curses of the soothsayer, they again threw themselves down the most dangerous cliffs. After the blessings of Balaam, or rather of God (for the words did not come from Balaam's own choice but from the power that moved him), they committed fornication with the daughters of foreigners and were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor. When Moses saw such shame and such a mockery, he again ordered them to cut one another down, saying, "Each of you kill his neighbor who has been initiated into Baal of Peor." It was as if a wound had received many incisions and cauterizations and was no better for it, and someone ordered the rest of it to be cut and burned again. When you hear of these hardships, do not think they were the only ones that happened. I have left out not a few of those recorded: the wars, the attacks of enemies, the long journeys, his sister's insolence and her punishment, which grieved that most gentle Moses even more. Yet even if someone gathered all of it together with care, what is written is not a ten-thousandth part of what happened. For if one of the servants… [?]

…to be constantly engaged in [wars] and battles? What soul would such a life have allowed to be at rest? Even if he went on winning, his worry about what remained to be done spoiled the pleasure of his victories. The distribution of the allotments also gave him much toil and many difficulties. Anyone knows this who has been appointed to divide even a modest estate among brothers, or among someone's heirs from another branch of the family. I do not think I need to speak of the people's later disasters. The question before us now is not whether someone led a painful life, but whether someone who greatly pleased God did.

6. So, if you agree, let us pass over Eli. He is among those who gave offense, because of his sons' wickedness, or rather because of his own negligence. He was punished not because he had wicked sons, but because he was more lenient than he should have been and did not defend God's laws when they were outraged. He recognized this himself after the severe threat, and said, "It is the Lord; he will do what is good in his sight." So let us pass him by and come to Samuel. Samuel was raised in the temple from childhood and always found favor before God. He showed such virtue from his earliest years that he was counted among the marvelous prophets before he reached manhood, and this at a time when prophecy had failed. "For there was," it says, "no clear vision, and the word was precious." This Samuel, then, who was born after many tears, first saw his teacher carried off by that pitiable death, and he was as confused and troubled as a grateful and affectionate disciple would be. After this he was continually forced to lament the disasters of the Jews. His sons were unjust and depraved and went to the utmost wickedness. They grieved him both by this and by being unable to inherit the honor given to him. This dejection was followed (or rather not followed, since it did not end, but added to) by the lawless request of the Israelites. At that point he was so cast down that he needed much consolation. Hear, then, what God says to him: "It is not you they have despised, but me." Yet even after this he cared for them so much that he said to them, "Far be it from me to sin by ceasing to pray for you." Seeing those he loved so much faring badly, stumbling in wars and provoking God, what pleasure could he have felt? What time could he have spent without dejection and tears? When he had made Saul king, pains were again heaped on him, one after another and without a break. Saul offered the sacrifice against what seemed good to God. And when he had conquered the Amalekites, he spared their king, and that against the command. Samuel was so stricken in soul by this that he never saw the man again, but mourned and wept for him from then until his last day. He was even rebuked for the excess of his dejection: "How long," it says, "will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him?" If he mourned at these things, what must it have been like when that man slaughtered so many priests for no reason and to no purpose? When he came a second time to kill his benefactor, who had done him no wrong? When he saw him naked…

…[?] taking upon himself the blame for so great a slaughter, [?] and having made covenants with him on behalf of many [?] at the time when he [was to] repay him for his kindnesses [?], he lived a life more wretched than any wrongdoer. Even if nothing else had troubled him, it was enough to wound and destroy a soul to count himself the slayer of so many priests. This thought struck him and gnawed at his soul night and day more than a moth, and then he received other wounds in succession, continual and one after another. When Nabal insulted him through his servants and called him a runaway, a fugitive and an ungrateful slave, he did not bear the words without pain. And when he went to Achish and pretended to be mad, he fell down, rolled his eyes, and let much foam run from his mouth. He was wasting away more than people who are truly possessed, as he considered what straits he had brought himself to, he who had received so many benefits. When he had a little respite among the enemy, he was expected to march against their enemies. But the satraps envied him and wanted to slander him to the king, so they sent him away from the army as useless to them, as a plotter and a likely traitor. "For the satraps of the Philistines," it says, "were angry with him and said to him: Send the man back, and let him return to the place where you set him. Do not let him come with us to war, or become a plotter in the camp. With what will this man reconcile himself to his lord, if not with the heads of these men?" Struck by these words, he withdrew with much humiliation and dejection. When he came home, he found such evils there that he was almost choked with grief. The troubles that happened then would have been enough to darken his soul even if he had seen them coming. But because they were unexpected and beyond all anticipation, they seemed twice as great as they were and were no longer bearable. He was going home as if to rest, expecting to find consolation for his dejection in his children and his wives. But on arriving he suddenly heard that they were slaves among the enemy, and he saw fire and smoke and blood and corpses. Before he could grieve for them and lament their captivity, the people living in the city fell upon him more fiercely than wild beasts, each of them seeking consolation for his own losses from David's head. When contrary winds fall upon the sea, a great and wild storm rises from their battle. So it was then: as dejection and fear tore at the righteous man's soul, the surge and the tumult were great, these passions in turn overpowering and being overpowered without pause. He managed to get through these evils and to recover his wives and all the captives. But before he could even feel that victory, he was struck by bitter news, the slaughter of Jonathan. How this cast down his soul can be learned from his laments: "Your love fell upon me," he says, "like the love of women." And why do I speak of the laments? He wept like this for Jonathan's father, his own enemy, who plotted against him and wished for his destruction ten thousand times. What then must he have suffered for the one who stood by him in those dangers, who often rescued him from his father's plots, who shared his secrets,

…house, and to send her through the marketplace crying and lamenting. When Absalom learned of this, he invited all his brothers to a meal. Among them was the one who had committed the outrage, and in the middle of the feasting and drinking Absalom had him slaughtered by his servants. Then someone got up and left, and because of the uproar he did not learn clearly what had happened. He reported to the king that all his sons were dead. And the king sat lamenting the murder of them all, which had not happened. When he learned the truth, he threatened his son and said he would kill him. Absalom fled and spent three years in a foreign land, and David remained angry that whole time. He would not have called him back even then, had not the wisdom of his general thrust him into giving that promise against his will. But even when he had called him back, he did not quench the wound in his heart. He kept him away from his presence for two more years, and only after this long time, when the general pleaded again, did he grant him access. Then Absalom, either holding a grudge over this or simply lusting for power, rose up against his father. He drove him back into the wanderings and flights he had endured under Saul, or rather made this time far harder than that one. Back then he had suffered these things as a general. Now, after many years on the throne and after conquering practically all his enemies, he was forced to flee. And the one who forced him was not a stranger or an enemy, but one who, as he himself lamented, came forth from his own body. Back then he was in the prime of life and could bear everything nobly. Now, at the wrong time of life, when he ought to have been cared for in his old age by that abominable man, he was plotted against and attacked. The king went out with a few men, barefoot, his head covered, weeping. The war brought him not only misfortune but shame. The son treated that blessed man so much more insolently than Saul had that he violated his father's concubines. He did it not in secret but on the roof, with everyone watching. In his mad rage against his father he outraged the ordinances of nature and the laws of sexual union. Drunk with folly, while the war was still going on, he dared to do and to display what belongs to those who have already won and taken their opponents captive. Ziba found David in this state of anguish and fear and troubled him further by lying about his master, saying that he had taken the usurper's side.

9. After him came Shimei, a vile and ungrateful man. He pelted David with countless insults, and with stones too, along with these words: "Get out, you man of blood, you lawless man! The Lord has brought back on you all the blood of the house of Saul, because you reigned in his place. The Lord has given the kingdom into the hands of your son Absalom and has shown you your wickedness, for you are a man of blood." David was wasting away as he heard and suffered these things, as he showed by his very laments. Yet he dared do nothing more. He said, "Let him curse, for the Lord has told him to, so that he may see my humiliation, and the Lord may repay me with good in place of the curse on this day." And he let him go away alive. He himself waited, anxious about how things stood with Hushai and trembling over what would happen [?]… thousands of men in half a day's time, when he also utters those pitiable words [?]…

[?] king. For when he saw the angel with his sword drawn, he said, "Behold, I the shepherd have sinned, and I the shepherd have done wrong; but these, the flock [?] (for that manner of death surpasses every calamity [?]), what have they done? Let your hand be upon me and upon my father's house." Now, we cannot recount all his sorrows exactly, because not all of them are recorded. But from his laments and his wailing we can guess how great the omitted ones were too, and see that the righteous man never stopped beating his breast and grieving. For what does he say? "The days of our years, in them are seventy years; and if in strength, eighty years; and the greater part of them is toil and trouble." If you say that he condemned the common life of all and not only his own, you are saying something greater than I mean to say myself, and you spare us many words. You admit yourself that neither his life nor anyone else's can be found that does not hold far more hardship than good. Indeed, as you yourself rightly said, he considered not only his own affairs but those of others too before he pronounced this verdict. [218] He said the same as the patriarch, but with greater force: what the patriarch declared about his own case, David later declared about all. The one said, "Few and evil are my days"; but the other, "The days of our years, in them are seventy years" (that is, the years of all human beings), "and the greater part of them is toil and trouble."

10. But, as I said, I leave these things for you to go through carefully at your leisure. I will come to the remaining prophets. They nowhere left us a written account of their lives. Yet they too fell into such great distress, because of the overwhelming evils that held them fast, that I think I can show from a single word that their whole life was full of pain. First comes what was common to them all: they spent their entire lives tortured, scourged, sawn in two, stoned, imprisoned, dying by the sword, going about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated. Besides this, they had a further cause of sorrow, harder still: they saw the wickedness of those who treated them so growing worse, and this stung them more than their own afflictions. One said, "Cursing and lying, theft and adultery and murder have flooded the land, and they mix blood with blood," showing us how fearless, how intricate and how plentiful the wickedness was. Another cried out in turn, "Woe is me! For I have become like one gathering stubble at harvest, like a gleaning at the vintage when there is no cluster," lamenting in these words how scarce good men were. Another again bewailed other things of the same kind. The goatherd not only mourned their wickedness but lamented their calamities more than his own trials, and he besought God, saying, "Be merciful, Lord; who will raise up Jacob? For he is very small. Repent, Lord, concerning this." Yet not even so did he obtain what he asked, for God said, "And it shall not be, says the Lord." And Isaiah, when he heard that the whole land would be desolate, would not even be comforted, [?] [Textual notes: ἱκετηρίας ("supplication") is the correct reading, Morel; σωτηρίας ("salvation") [?] Morel. ἀεὶ στρεφόμενος ("always turning about"), Savile and Colbert MS; ἀναστρεφόμενος ("living, conducting himself").]

[?] he saw, and the temple defiled by the sacrifices and made desolate, and all holiness overturned. So he mourned and wept, saying, "To us belongs shame of face, and to our kings, our rulers and our fathers, because we have sinned against you, the Lord."

11. But somehow, among the prophets, I passed over that soul as high as heaven, the man who lived on earth as though in heaven, for he owned nothing beyond his sheepskin cloak. What, then, did this great and wonderful man do, if we should even call him a man? After his bold words to Ahab, after calling down fire, after slaughtering the priests, after shutting and opening heaven for as long as he wished in each case, after so many great achievements, he was so overcome by fear and by overwhelming despondency that he uttered these words: [220] "Take my life from me, for I am no better than my fathers." This was said by the man who has not died even now. And not only this: he went off into the wilderness and slept there, bowed down by heaviness of spirit. His disciple received from his teacher not only a double portion of the spirit but also far greater afflictions. Blessed Paul showed us these men a little while ago, listing their miseries, and said, "of whom the world was not worthy." This blessed man has come in upon us at just the right moment. Even if he had been seen alone he would have been enough to console us; coming in after the others, what despondency and grief would he not banish? I think there is no need to speak of his hunger and thirst and nakedness, his shipwrecks, his times in deserts, his fears and dangers, the plots, the prisons, the blows, the sleepless nights, the countless deaths [?], and everything else he endured for the sake of preaching. For though these brought him some afflictions, they also gave him joys. But when all those in Asia turned away from him, when the Galatians were led astray, a whole nation and one of good repute, when the Corinthians split their church into many factions and, by flattering the fornicator, brought him to insensibility, what do you think he suffered? What darkness gripped his soul? But why do we need to reason it out, when we can hear his own words? Writing to the Corinthians he said, "Out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears"; and again, "lest when I come God humble me, and I mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented." And to the Galatians, "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you." About the people of Asia he laments to his disciple. And it was not only these things that grieved him: the thorn given to him so afflicted and distressed him that he begged God many times to be freed from it, for "three times" here means "often." Indeed, when could he ever breathe freely, a man who beat his breast even at the absence of a brother? "Because I did not find Titus my brother," he says, "I had no rest." And again he suffered the same over an illness: "For God had mercy on him," he says (concerning [?] [Textual notes: [?] Colbert MS. τοῦτο πάσχων ("suffering this"). πολλῷ τούτων μείζονα ("far greater than these"), Savile in the margin. πολλῷ [?]]

[?] loss of money, you must not assume that others are affected the same way. For the loss of these things has driven many even to derangement and to utter ruin. Neither of these can overthrow a noble soul; but a weak soul, more attached to worldly things, is stung by that more than by this. Why so? Because constantly fearing starvation is not the same as being troubled for a few days by this disease. Here all the violence is confined to a short span of time, as when a fever or a chill or some other recurring fit strikes, or rather it lasts much less time than these. And if it is worse in its violence, I could show you many fever patients far more out of their minds than the demon-possessed, when they are gripped by that fire. [222] But the fear of want, of lacking necessities, sits constantly by the soul of the poor like a never-ending moth and eats it away. And why speak of poverty? If we chose to count up all human calamities, you yourself, and not only we, would perhaps laugh at your own laments and groans. We cannot tell them all, or rather not even a tiny fraction of them, for we do not know them, and even if we did, all of time would not suffice for the telling. But I will pick out a few from many, and from these I will help you, as far as I can, to guess at the ones left unmentioned. Remember that dear old man, Demophilus I mean, of the great and illustrious house. For fifteen years now he has been no better off than the dead as far as doing anything is concerned, except that he trembles constantly, speaks, and has a clear awareness of his own sufferings. He lives in extreme poverty and has a single young man to serve him, who is good and devoted to his master, but not able to relieve that calamity. He can neither ward off the poverty nor stop the trembling of the paralysis. All he can do is put a morsel into his master's mouth (for the old man's hands cannot help him even with this), hold a cup to his lips, and wipe his nose when he has a cold; beyond these he can do nothing more. This man, then, has been suffering this way for fifteen years now, as I said; but I am also thinking of the one who spent thirty-eight years in this affliction. And consider, besides these, Aristoxenus the Bithynian. His body is not broken down like that old man's, but a disease far harsher than that paralysis lies upon him. In his belly come certain spasms, and pains more bitter than any agony, at times piercing him worse than spits, at times gnawing at him more fiercely than fire. They torment him every day and every night, and to those who do not know his illness they give him the look of a madman: they so twist his eyes and so wrench his hands and feet that they leave him unable to speak. His shrieks and wails (for after that speechlessness he often cries out) outdo the screams of women in labor. Often people living far off who had sick folk at home, troubled by long sleeplessness, have sent to complain on behalf of their sufferers, saying they were worse off from the [?] [Textual notes: Savile: μόνον ("only") [?]. Savile: ἐν αὐτοῖς … αὐτοῖς ἐστιν.]

[?] they have the pain. If you do not believe it, that is no wonder. We do not usually judge our own troubles and other people's with the same mind. Others' troubles we learn of only by report and by sight, our own by experience and feeling and with our own sense of them. That is why we think ours harder to bear than theirs, [224] even if ours are quite light and bearable. But if someone who was free of all these troubles were to learn their nature and examine those who had fallen into them, he would cast an impartial vote on them for us. Perhaps you will say that all those sufferings concern only the body, while this disease of yours touches the soul and is harsher than all of them. Yet it is precisely in this respect that we shall find it lighter than those. For this one does not even destroy the body, as they do, and it troubles the soul only for a short time. But the ones we have just listed spring up in the flesh, and do not confine their damage to it: they pass it on to the soul as well, torturing it without respite and corrupting it through pain and great despondency. "For as vinegar is harmful to a wound," it says, "so suffering that befalls the body grieves the heart." So do not just say that this is born of the body; show me that it does not pass on all its damage and corruption to the soul. Plague, too, is not born of our bodies, yet it destroys bodies; and the venom of reptiles comes from them, yet it harms us [?]. So it is with these sufferings: they are born of the body, but they pour the venom of their own evil into our soul. For an excess of despondency is more harmful than any working of a demon. Indeed the demon himself, over whomever he prevails, prevails through despondency; take it away, and no one will suffer anything terrible from him. "But how can one not be despondent?" you say. I will ask you in turn: how can one not keep from despondency? If you have dared adultery or murder, or some other such thing of the kind that shuts people out of the kingdom of heaven, then be despondent and mourn; no one will stop you. But if by the grace of God you stand far from all these, why beat your breast for nothing?

14. God placed despondency in our nature not so that we would use it at random, at the wrong time, and in the wrong circumstances, nor so that we would destroy ourselves, but so that we would gain the greatest benefits from it. How can we gain from it? When we take it up at the proper time. And the time for despondency is not when we suffer evil but when we do evil. But we have reversed the order and swapped the times: we do countless evils and do not shrink back even a little, yet if we suffer some small thing from anyone, we collapse, grow dizzy, and hasten to be rid of life and depart from it. That is why the thing seems burdensome and heavy to us, as do anger and desire. For those who did not use these well or as they ought have brought them into disrepute. The same thing happens as with the medicines doctors prescribe; and [?] [Textual notes: Colbert MS: ἐπέτριψε ("crushed, ruined"), perhaps ἐπέτρεψε ("permitted"). Colbert MS: πάλιν ("again"); others: πολλήν ("much").]

[?] you are in pain. "And how is it clear," you say, "that we are not paying this penalty for our offenses?" It is perfectly plain [?] that this is an occasion for crowns and for a greater [reward?], but for now I do not insist on this. Let it be granted, if you like, that it is not unclear, as you said, but entirely clear that this is a requital for sins. Is that why you are grieving, tell me? Yet it is reason for good cheer to settle our sins here and not be condemned with the world. A person who grieves should grieve not over what he is punished for, but over the sins by which he provokes God. Sins separate God from us and make him our enemy, but punishments reconcile him to us and make him merciful and near. That this sweat and toil is not a requital for sins but an occasion for crowns and prizes is clear from the following. If you had lived your earlier life shamefully and dissolutely, and had then moved over to the monastic way of life, not even then would there be grounds for this suspicion. For if God brings punishments in order to turn the stubborn to repentance, then once repentance has been shown, punishment is superfluous from then on, at least for this purpose. God is so far from wanting to punish us that often, even when we do things that deserve punishment and need much correction, he chastens us with threats and fearful words alone. You can see this in the case of Israel and of the city of the Ninevites. When they showed repentance, he not only did not bring the punishment but at once cancelled the threat as well. He wants us to suffer no harm far more than we want it for ourselves, and no one would spare himself as God spares all of us. So would he who frightens with words, and does not punish, those who have often sinned, and who frees them even from that anguish once they repent, not only refuse to free you from the threat, you who have shown such piety and virtue, but actually hand you over to punishment in deed? How could anyone believe this? Even so, if your earlier life had been corrupt and wicked, as I said, someone might be able to entertain the thought. But now, [?] though that life was less [perfect] than your present one, it too was orderly and full of much [?] [?] but once you have trained yourself well in them, you will from now on be proof against all the sorrows of life.
